slides.narration: In this part of Chapter 7, use 7.1.2 Building do-while Loops as an engineering claim, not a vocabulary word. A do-while loop executes its body before testing the condition, so it runs at least once. It fits a menu that must be displayed before asking whether to repeat, but it is wrong when an empty collection should cause no work. The syntax ends with a semicolon after the condition. Choose this form because one initial execution is required, not because it saves a line. In interactive code, a failed input operation must still be handled; repeatedly displaying a prompt does not repair a failed stream. Keep the termination decision and the input-consumption rule together so that the loop cannot become an endless series of prompts over unchanged invalid input. slides.title: 7.2.1 Building Traditional for Loops
keyPoints: A traditional for loop groups initialization, continuation condition, and iteration update in one place.
The idiom for (std::size_t i = 0; i < size; ++i) visits the half-open interval [0, size).
The strict less-than comparison is important: index size is already beyond the last element.
Use a type and direction that make the bounds safe.
slides.narration: In this part of Chapter 7, use 7.2.1 Building Traditional for Loops as an engineering claim, not a vocabulary word. A traditional for loop groups initialization, continuation condition, and iteration update in one place. The idiom for (std::size_t i = 0; i < size; ++i) visits the half-open interval [0, size). The strict less-than comparison is important: index size is already beyond the last element. Use a type and direction that make the bounds safe. An unsigned index cannot become negative in the way a signed countdown might expect, so a condition such as i >= 0 never becomes false for an unsigned value. For reverse traversal, use a suitable iterator or a carefully stated half-open pattern rather than relying on underflow as an exit mechanism. The graduate-level move is to ask what evidence would make the claim trustworthy: a compiler diagnostic, a runtime value, a preserved invariant, or a boundary that failed cleanly. slides.narration: In this part of Chapter 7, use 7.2.2 Using Range-Based for Loops as an engineering claim, not a vocabulary word. A range-based loop visits each element of a range without exposing the traversal machinery. for (int value : values) copies each integer into the loop variable. for (auto& value : values) can modify existing elements, while const auto& observes them without copying larger objects or permitting modification through that reference. Do not structurally modify a vector during a range-based traversal unless you have carefully established the iterator-validity rules. Appending may reallocate storage and invalidate the loop’s hidden iterators. A loop that only transforms existing elements is simpler. Choose an index loop when positions are genuinely part of the algorithm, not merely because indexing is familiar. slides.title: Trace the invariant
keyPoints: Before each iteration, sum equals the total of accepted readings already visited, and accepted equals their count.
The marker branch exits without altering either.
The negative branch skips without altering either.
The accepting branch adds exactly one value and increments the count once.
slides.narration: In this part of Chapter 7, use Trace the invariant as an engineering claim, not a vocabulary word. Before each iteration, sum equals the total of accepted readings already visited, and accepted equals their count. The marker branch exits without altering either. The negative branch skips without altering either. The accepting branch adds exactly one value and increments the count once. That is the invariant the loop preserves. At termination, four values have been accepted: four, seven, zero, and nine. The sum is twenty. Zero contributes no amount but does contribute one accepted observation. That detail catches a common mistake in which “nonzero” is confused with “valid.” The graduate-level move is to ask what evidence would make the claim trustworthy: a compiler diagnostic, a runtime value, a preserved invariant, or a boundary that failed cleanly. slides.narration: In this part of Chapter 7, use Failure clinic — The loop that never reaches the next item as an engineering claim, not a vocabulary word. Rewrite a small scan as a while loop in a copy. Place the index increment after a branch that can continue. When that branch is taken, the index does not advance. Do not leave this broken program running indefinitely; reason through the repeated state or use a bounded diagnostic version that stops after a small number of iterations. The repair is not to add an arbitrary sleep or increase a timeout. The progress state is wrong. Move or redesign the update so every continuing path advances appropriately, or use a loop form whose update naturally expresses the invariant. slides.title: What is the key difference between while and do-while?
keyPoints: Answer first, reveal second
Support the answer with evidence
Name the boundary or invariant involved
Connect the answer to source, output, or diagnostics
slides.narration: Use this checkpoint as a pressure test. The learner should answer before seeing the provided explanation: What is the key difference between while and do-while? The supplied answer is: while checks before the body and may run zero times. do-while checks after the body and runs at least once.. Do not let the session end with memorized phrasing. Ask for the evidence. In this chapter, evidence means source-level mechanism, runtime output, diagnostic behavior, preserved state, or an acceptance condition.
actions: Give learners thirty seconds to answer before opening the details disclosure.
When revealing the answer, require one sentence of evidence, not just the label of the concept.
Connect the answer back to the chapter's code or acceptance boundary.

slides.title: Close the lecture with evidence
keyPoints: Restate the chapter contract
Name the most important output or invariant
Separate normal output from diagnostics
Assign a small edit-and-explain task
slides.narration: Close Chapter 7 by having learners restate the chapter in one engineering sentence. For Repeating Operations with Loops, that sentence should include the mechanism, the boundary, and the evidence. Then ask for the thing most likely to fool a beginner: confusing a printed value with correctness, ignoring stderr, assuming exit status proves output, or trusting a diagram without checking code. The homework move is small but serious: make one controlled change, predict the new output, run it, and write the explanation in terms of source behavior.
actions: Return to the chapter Outline and point learners to Code & labs for the source files.
Assign one controlled edit to the interactive lab and require a written output explanation.
Tell learners to export lecture work if they modified code during the session.

question.answer: A short explanation that connects chapter vocabulary to source code, observed output, diagnostics or their absence, exit status, and any preserved invariant.
